questions.statement: Which sentence best introduces an opinion in a short article?
questions.context: A student writes a short article for the school newspaper about school routines.

options.text: In my view, homework should be reduced.
options.feedback: Correct! 'In my view' clearly marks a personal position, which is what an opinion paragraph requires.

options.text: The weather was warm in March.
options.feedback: 'The weather was warm' states a fact and expresses no opinion.

options.text: Homework is a form of study.
options.feedback: 'Homework is a form of study' is a definition and takes no position.

options.text: The teacher gave homework on Monday.
options.feedback: 'The teacher gave homework' reports an event and supports no argument.

questions.explanation:
An opinion must be signalled as an opinion. A phrase such as 'in my view' or 'I believe' tells the reader that a position follows.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which phrase best softens a strong opinion in academic writing?
questions.context: A student writes an argumentative paragraph for a language exam and must avoid absolute statements.

options.feedback: 'It is obvious that' removes any possibility of discussion, which is the opposite of hedging.
Correct! 'It could be argued that' presents a claim as one that can be defended, which is the academic way to qualify a position.
'Everyone knows that' claims universal agreement without evidence.
'There is no doubt that' states certainty and admits no counterargument.

questions.explanation:
Hedges such as 'could be argued', 'tends to' and 'may' keep a claim open to discussion, which is what academic style requires.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which connective is most suitable to add a supporting reason?
questions.context: A student develops an opinion paragraph and needs to extend the argument without contradicting it.

options.feedback: 'However' contrasts two ideas, and the sentence continues the same line of argument.
'Therefore' presents a consequence, which is not the function of an added reason.
Correct! 'Moreover' adds a second point that strengthens the first.
'In contrast' introduces an opposing idea and would break the flow of support.

questions.explanation:
Each connective declares a different relationship between clauses, and choosing the wrong one changes the meaning of the paragraph.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which sentence is an appropriate concluding sentence for an opinion paragraph?
questions.context: A student closes a short opinion piece about school homework.

options.text: Homework is often given on Fridays.
options.feedback: 'Homework is often given on Fridays' is a fact and closes no argument.
'The term has twenty weeks' is background information, not a closing position.

options.text: Some teachers give less homework than others.
options.feedback: 'Some teachers give less homework' is a secondary observation and does not close the argument.

options.text: For these reasons, homework should be limited to one subject.
options.feedback: Correct! The sentence gathers the reasons and restates the position, which is the function of a conclusion.

questions.explanation:
A conclusion refers back to the reasons already given, so it uses a phrase such as 'for these reasons' before repeating the position.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which word best links a concession to an opinion paragraph?
questions.context: A student wants to acknowledge the strongest argument against a position before answering it.

options.feedback: Correct! 'Although' introduces a point against the writer's own position and sets up a reply.
'Therefore' presents a consequence, not an opposing point.
'Also' adds a supporting point and creates no contrast.
'Besides' adds extra information and also creates no contrast.

questions.explanation:
Concession makes a paragraph stronger. A writer who states the opposite view and answers it appears balanced and credible.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which sentence avoids an unsupported generalisation?
questions.context: A student reports on a school project and must keep the claims within the evidence gathered.

options.text: All students always finish their work quickly.
options.feedback: 'All students always' claims knowledge of every student without evidence.

options.text: In the two classes I observed, most students finished on time.
options.feedback: Correct! The sentence limits the claim to the classes actually observed, which is what evidence supports.

options.text: Students never finish their work on time.
options.feedback: 'Never' denies something the writer has not tested.

options.text: Every student is lazy about homework.
options.feedback: 'Every student is lazy' is a value judgement presented as a fact.

questions.explanation:
Quantifying the scope of a claim, as in 'in the two classes I observed', is what keeps an opinion paragraph defensible.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which phrase is used to introduce a counterargument?
questions.context: A student presents an argument and then wishes to acknowledge what other people say.

options.feedback: 'For example' introduces an illustration of the previous point.
'In addition' adds supporting information.
Correct! 'Some people argue that' explicitly presents a position held by others.
'As a result' introduces a consequence.

questions.explanation:
Naming who holds a position makes the disagreement visible to the reader, which a simple contrastive connective alone does not do.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which verb is used to present a position in a formal essay?
questions.context: A student writes an essay in a formal register for an examination.

options.feedback: 'Shout' is informal and describes a volume of voice, not an argument.
'Happen' describes an event and cannot take a clause as its object in this sense.
'Belong' expresses membership, not the holding of an opinion.
Correct! 'Maintain' means to hold firmly to a position, which fits the register of a formal essay.

questions.explanation:
Register is part of the mark. A formal essay avoids informal verbs and prefers words such as 'maintain', 'assert' or 'contend'.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which structure best presents a contrast of two positions?
questions.context: A student sets out two views about the school timetable before giving a personal position.

options.text: While some people favour longer hours, others believe breaks are essential.
options.feedback: Correct! The structure 'while ... others' sets two positions side by side and marks the contrast explicitly.

options.text: Longer hours are common in many schools.
options.feedback: The second sentence states one position alone and creates no contrast.
The third sentence supports one side and ignores the disagreement.

options.text: Some schools have longer days than others.
options.feedback: The fourth sentence compares schools rather than positions.

questions.explanation:
A balanced essay presents both sides explicitly, and a correlative structure makes the disagreement readable in a single sentence.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which connective best introduces a consequence of the writer's own opinion?
questions.context: A student develops an argument and wants to describe what would follow if the proposal were accepted.

options.feedback: 'Nevertheless' introduces a contrast that works against the previous idea.
Correct! 'As a result' introduces what follows from the position stated.
'For example' introduces a case that illustrates the idea.
'On the other hand' contrasts two positions.

questions.explanation:
Writing clearly means naming the relationship between two sentences. A consequence needs a result connective, not a contrastive one.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which sentence correctly uses a modal to express an opinion about a proposal?
questions.context: A student writes a proposal for the school improvement plan.

options.text: Schools must to offer more activities after class.
options.feedback: 'Must to' adds an infinitive marker after a modal, which is not allowed.

options.text: Schools should offering more activities after class.
options.feedback: 'Should offering' places a gerund after a modal, which is not a possible form.

options.text: Schools should offer more activities after class.
options.feedback: Correct! 'Should' is the modal of advice and it is followed by the base form of the verb.

options.text: Schools are should offer more activities after class.
options.feedback: 'Are should' places two auxiliaries in a single clause.

questions.explanation:
The modal carries the recommendation and the base form follows it, which is the fixed pattern of all modal verbs in English.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which expression would a writer use to qualify a claim without weakening it too much?
questions.context: A student reviews a paragraph in which several claims were too absolute.

options.feedback: 'Always' extends a claim to every case, which the evidence rarely supports.
'Never' denies a claim completely.
'Without exception' states that no case is different, which is an absolute claim.
Correct! 'Generally speaking' limits the scope of a claim while leaving it clear.

questions.explanation:
Qualifiers protect the credibility of a paragraph. Over-qualifying removes the force of the position the writer is trying to defend.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which topic sentence best suits an opinion paragraph about the value of reading?
questions.context: A student plans the topic sentence of a paragraph for a written exam.

options.text: Reading widely gives students a wider view of the world.
options.feedback: Correct! The sentence states a position and gives a reason that the rest of the paragraph can develop.

options.text: Reading is an activity many people do.
options.feedback: 'Reading is an activity' is a definition and takes no position.
'Some students read' reports a habit and supports no argument.
'The library opens at eight' is background information about a building.

questions.explanation:
A topic sentence in an opinion paragraph contains the position itself, so the rest of the paragraph has a clear claim to support.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which sentence avoids an empty generalisation in an opinion essay?
questions.context: A student compares two schools in a report and must keep the claims within what was actually measured.

options.text: Libraries are important in every school in the world.
options.feedback: 'Every school in the world' is a claim about the whole planet with no evidence behind it.

options.text: In the two schools I visited, reading scores were higher where libraries stayed open late.
options.feedback: Correct! The sentence names the number of schools observed and the specific comparison made, which is evidence.
'Sometimes' is too vague to support any argument.
'Every year' is a trend claim that the sentence does not evidence.

questions.explanation:
Naming the sample and the measure is what turns a generalisation into an argument a reader can check.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which word best expresses the writer's own conviction without overstating it?
questions.context: A student revises a paragraph so that the strength of the opinion matches the evidence available.

options.feedback: 'Allegedly' reports something that has not been verified and weakens the position.
'Presumably' marks the writer's own uncertainty about the claim.
Correct! 'Firmly' states conviction without claiming that the claim is beyond dispute.
'Apparently' also marks the writer's uncertainty, so neither word supports a position the writer holds.

questions.explanation:
Words such as 'allegedly' and 'apparently' add distance to a claim and weaken the force of a position the writer actually holds.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which sentence correctly links a reason to an opinion using a conjunction?
questions.context: A student supports a proposal for the school with a clear reason.

options.text: I support the proposal because of saves water.
options.feedback: 'Because of' must be followed by a noun or a gerund, not by a clause.

options.text: I support the proposal since of it saves water.
options.feedback: 'Since of' adds a preposition after a conjunction, which is not possible.

options.text: I support the proposal because it saved yesterday.
options.feedback: 'Saved' is the past, and the reason is a general property of the proposal rather than a past event.

options.text: I support the proposal because it saves water.
options.feedback: Correct! 'Because' is followed by a complete clause with a subject and a verb.

questions.explanation:
'Because' introduces a clause and 'because of' introduces a noun phrase. Mixing the two is a frequent error in written work.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which option describes a balanced opinion paragraph?
questions.context: A teacher explains the structure expected in a paragraph of a written examination.

options.text: It states a position, presents a reason against it and answers that reason.
options.feedback: Correct! A balanced paragraph contains a claim, a counterargument and the writer's reply to it.

options.text: It repeats the same idea four times in different words.
options.feedback: Repetition adds no information and weakens the paragraph.

options.text: It lists every fact about the topic without choosing one.
options.feedback: A paragraph must choose a position, and a list of facts is not an argument.

options.text: It begins and ends with the same sentence.
options.feedback: Repeating the opening and the closing can be effective, but without development it says nothing new.

questions.explanation:
Balance means the writer can state an opposing view and still justify the original one, which is what the answer to the counterargument does.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which phrase is the most natural way to begin an opinion essay with a position the reader may not share?
questions.context: A student begins an essay on a practice that most people support.

options.text: Group work is common in many schools.
options.feedback: The first sentence is a fact and takes no position.

options.text: While many people prefer group work, I believe individual study works better.
options.feedback: Correct! The concessive opening acknowledges the common view before stating a different position.
The third sentence is a personal anecdote, which is not a position on the practice.
The fourth sentence describes a room and does not address the practice at all.

questions.explanation:
Opening with a concession prepares the reader for a position that differs from the majority, which makes the argument more persuasive.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which sentence would a writer use to summarise several points already made?
questions.context: A student has developed four points and now needs to close the essay.

options.feedback: The first sentence gives a bare opinion with no reference to the reasons.
The second sentence introduces a new fact instead of summarising.

options.text: Taken together, these measures make the proposal worth supporting.
options.feedback: Correct! 'Taken together' signals that the sentence gathers the points already presented.

options.text: Some measures are cheap and some are not.
options.feedback: The fourth sentence restates a detail and closes no argument.

questions.explanation:
A concluding sentence refers back explicitly. Without that reference the conclusion reads as a new and unsupported claim.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which phrase would a writer avoid in a formal opinion essay?
questions.context: A student reviews a draft essay and identifies the language that does not match the required register.

options.text: This evidence suggests a clear pattern.
options.feedback: 'This evidence suggests' is a measured statement suited to formal writing.

options.text: On the whole, the case is strong.
options.feedback: 'On the whole' is a hedge that qualifies a claim in an academic register.
'Taken together' summarises points and suits a concluding sentence.

options.text: You know, it is a total disaster.
options.feedback: Correct! The informal filler and the colloquial intensifier do not belong in a formal written argument.

questions.explanation:
Register is assessed in writing. Informal fillers and colloquial intensifiers lower the quality of a formal argument even when the content is right.
---
questions.subject: ingles
